messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Difficulties using categorical() distribution
parts:
Stan doesn't generate samples when using

y ~ foo(theta);

It just increments the log density.

You have to marginalize out discrete parameters in Stan.
There are chapters in the manual for latent discrete parameters
and mixture models that have examples (and also HMMs in the
time-series chapter).

I didn't see where the variable r_ was being used in our
Stan program, so it's hard to provide concrete advice.

- Bob

The variable r_[] represents samples for the interval counts over time.  It is converted to theta[], which represents samples from the Gamma process, or the cumulative interval counts over time (also the cumulative intensity function for this interval grouped NHPP model).  All I want to do is sample from a categorical distribution for r_[], using my specified probability mass functions.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Difficulties using categorical() distribution
parts:
Stan simply doesn't "sample from a (categorical) distribution" other than
in generated quantities using (categorical)_rng functions.

Stan doesn't allow discrete parameters. If you have categorical
data, that's fine, you just write it like everything else. If
you want categorical parameters, you need to marginalize them out.
If you need categorical predictions, put them in the generated quantities
block.

- Bob

parts:
My use of the dcat distribution with JAGS/BUGS was simply a workaround to allow me to sample from a custom discrete distribution, aka. an approximated gamma process.  If I can't sample from custom discrete distributions in a Stan model, or somehow approximate sampling from them, I don't see how I can make it work.  These samples are necessary, as they're directly used to generate the mean value function inputs for the NHPP model's log-likelihood function.
Regards,
REub
On Wed, Feb 22, 2017 at 1:27 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

Stan simply doesn't "sample from a (categorical) distribution" other than
in generated quantities using (categorical)_rng functions.

Stan doesn't allow discrete parameters.  If you have categorical
data, that's fine, you just write it like everything else.  If
you want categorical parameters, you need to marginalize them out.
If you need categorical predictions, put them in the generated quantities
block.

- Bob

Stan simply doesn't "sample from a (categorical) distribution" other than
in generated quantities using (categorical)_rng functions.

Stan doesn't allow discrete parameters.  If you have categorical
data, that's fine, you just write it like everything else.  If
you want categorical parameters, you need to marginalize them out.
If you need categorical predictions, put them in the generated quantities
block.

parts:
Stan doesn't support discrete parameters. So you won't be able
to write your own discrete sampler. Or if you think you do, you'll
find it won't work in inference because the step functions involved
break derivatives.

You will be able to marginalize out, though.

You might write a simple normal mixture model in JAGS model like this:

z[n] ~ dbern(theta);
y[n] ~ dnorm(mu[z[n]], sigma[z[n]]);

In Stan, you need to marginalize out that z parameter. So you
write the same thing with no discrete parameters as:

target += log_sum_exp(log(theta) + normal_lpdf(y[n] | mu[1], sigma[1]),
log1m(theta) + normal_lpdf(y[n] | mu[2], sigma[2]));

Works the same way with more than two values for z.

It gives you the exact same inference on the parameters mu and sigma,
except it's a lot faster and a lot more robust (as in it can be more
than two orders of magnitude faster). No surprise---just a consequence
of the Rao-Blackwell theorem and the fact that discrete sampling tends to
be intractable in practice---it just mixes terribly if there are any
correlations and has a really hard time with tails.

You can reconstruct anything you need to do with z.
You can see this implicitly in the mixture formulation above, where
mu[1], sigma[1] and mu[2], sigma[2] are both used.

You can reconstruct everything you need in expectation. Specifically,
you can calculate Pr[z[n] == 1 | y]

Check out the manual chapter on latent discrete parameters to see how all
that works.

Or you could do the same marginalization in JAGS using the zeros trick.
Others have found this hugely sped up their state-space models with latent
discrete parameters.

- Bob

The parameter for this NHPP's model is a discrete stochastic process, the gamma process, that for this case is also the mean-value function for the NHPP.  I don't see how the marginalizing approach would work for this application. 

I do believe that it would be trivial to code a user-defined function for an inverse transform sampler that generates discrete values from the gamma process.  All that would need to be called from this custom function would be functions to query from a gamma variable's cdf and to generate random uniform numbers.  It would also necessitate performing the call to this custom function outside the bounds of the time steps in the main Stan model's sampling progression.  However, I have no idea on the level of work involved with making this capability available in Stan.

On Wed, Feb 22, 2017 at 4:37 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

Stan doesn't support discrete parameters.  So you won't be able
to write your own discrete sampler.  Or if you think you do, you'll
find it won't work in inference because the step functions involved
break derivatives.

You will be able to marginalize out, though.

You might write a simple normal mixture model in JAGS model like this:

  z[n] ~ dbern(theta);
  y[n] ~ dnorm(mu[z[n]], sigma[z[n]]);

In Stan, you need to marginalize out that z parameter.  So you
write the same thing with no discrete parameters as:

  target += log_sum_exp(log(theta) + normal_lpdf(y[n] | mu[1], sigma[1]),
                        log1m(theta) + normal_lpdf(y[n] | mu[2], sigma[2]));

Works the same way with more than two values for z.

It gives you the exact same inference on the parameters mu and sigma,
except it's a lot faster and a lot more robust (as in it can be more
than two orders of magnitude faster).  No surprise---just a consequence
of the Rao-Blackwell theorem and the fact that discrete sampling tends to
be intractable in practice---it just mixes terribly if there are any
correlations and has a really hard time with tails.

You can reconstruct anything you need to do with z.
You can see this implicitly in the mixture formulation above, where
mu[1], sigma[1] and mu[2], sigma[2] are both used.

You can reconstruct everything you need in expectation.  Specifically,
you can calculate Pr[z[n] == 1 | y]

Check out the manual chapter on latent discrete parameters to see how all
that works.

Or you could do the same marginalization in JAGS using the zeros trick.
Others have found this hugely sped up their state-space models with latent
discrete parameters.

- Bob

parts:
> On Feb 22, 2017, at 7:22 PM, Reuben Johnston <reuben.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The parameter for this NHPP's model is a discrete stochastic process, the gamma process, that for this case is also the mean-value function for the NHPP. I don't see how the marginalizing approach would work for this application.

Does the gamma process have correlated outputs at each time
state like a Gaussian process or are the outputs conditionally
independent based on the discrete states like an HMM?

If it's the latter, it'd work like the forward algorithm in HMMs.
If it's the former, you're probably out of luck because the
margninalization will be intractable.

I had a hard time seeing the overall structure of the process from
your code. But then I didn't understand the Wikipedia page on
Gamma processes either.

> I do believe that it would be trivial to code a user-defined function for an inverse transform sampler that generates discrete values from the gamma process. All that would need to be called from this custom function would be functions to query from a gamma variable's cdf and to generate random uniform numbers. It would also necessitate performing the call to this custom function outside the bounds of the time steps in the main Stan model's sampling progression. However, I have no idea on the level of work involved with making this capability available in Stan.

You could code that, but you can't call random number generators in
Stan's model block---only after the fact in generated quantities. The
reason we do this is because they don't play nicely with inference.
They basically perform something like the "cut" in BUGS implicitly.
We lose the information connection statistically and we lose the
derivative information computationally.

- Bob

I am using the counting process, non-stationary form of the Gamma process and I think of it as being very similar to the non-homogeneous Poisson process, but the interarrival times are gamma distributed, rather than exponential (as in the NHPP).  A more formal definition is provided by van Noortwijk:

"Let v(t) be a non-decreasing, right-continuous,real-valued function for t>=0, with v(0)=0. The gamma process with shape function v(t)>0 and scale parameter u>0 is a continuous-time stochastic process {X(t),t>=0} with the following properties:
(1) X(0)=0 with probability one;
(2) X(tau)-X(t)~Ga(v(tau)-v(t),u), for all tau>t>=0;
(3) X(t) has independent increments

Pages 8-10 of 2007, Merrick and Soyer provide the best description of how I am using the gamma process.  It will also be described in my dissertation, but that is not finished yet.  A very concise description is as follows.

I estimated the values for the Gamma process's probability mass function and passed in the results for a subset of the realizations (e.g., pr(Θ(t)=n, for n=1:250) as an array to BUGS/JAGS.  I then used the dcat() distribution with this pmf, to simulate values from the Gamma process prior (i.e., dcat provides samples from Θ(t) in the range 1<=N<=250, according to the probabilities in the pmf passed to dcat), in the sampling steps in BUGS/JAGS.  In this model, the parameter Θ(t) is used as the cumulative intensity (or mean-value) function for a non-homogeneous Poisson process.  For this alternative, the prior for Θ(t)~GammaProcess(c*Λ(t),c), where the hyper-parameter Λ(t) is described as a best guess for the NHPP mean value function and c is a constant describing the measure of certainty for the best guess given the prior history, where lower values indicate higher confidence in the best guess.  I am using the counting form of the NHPP, so my data are grouped-interval counts over time.  An example dataset for the intervals t=(0-10], (10-20], (20-30], would be the respective cumulative counts 10, 25, and 50.

References:
* 2008, Merrick, Soyer, Computational Issues in Semiparametric Bayesian Replacement Models, Technical Report TR-2008-4
* 2007, Merrick, Soyer, Semiparametric Bayesian Decision Models for Optimal Replacement, Technical Report TR-2007-4
* 2007, van Noortwijk, A survey of the application of gamma processes in maintenance

> I do believe that it would be trivial to code a user-defined function for an inverse transform sampler that generates discrete values from the gamma process.  All that would need to be called from this custom function would be functions to query from a gamma variable's cdf and to generate random uniform numbers.  It would also necessitate performing the call to this custom function outside the bounds of the time steps in the main Stan model's sampling progression.  However, I have no idea on the level of work involved with making this capability available in Stan.

You could code that, but you can't call random number generators in
Stan's model block---only after the fact in generated quantities.  The
reason we do this is because they don't play nicely with inference.
They basically perform something like the "cut" in BUGS implicitly.
We lose the information connection statistically and we lose the
derivative information computationally.

> I am using the counting process, non-stationary form of the Gamma process and I think of it as being very similar to the non-homogeneous Poisson process, but the interarrival times are gamma distributed, rather than exponential (as in the NHPP). A more formal definition is provided by van Noortwijk:
>
> "Let v(t) be a non-decreasing, right-continuous,real-valued function for t>=0, with v(0)=0. The gamma process with shape function v(t)>0 and scale parameter u>0 is a continuous-time stochastic process {X(t),t>=0} with the following properties:
> (1) X(0)=0 with probability one;
> (2) X(tau)-X(t)~Ga(v(tau)-v(t),u), for all tau>t>=0;
> (3) X(t) has independent increments
>
> Pages 8-10 of 2007, Merrick and Soyer provide the best description of how I am using the gamma process. It will also be described in my dissertation, but that is not finished yet. A very concise description is as follows.

> I estimated the values for the Gamma process's probability mass function and passed in the results for a subset of the realizations (e.g., pr(Θ(t)=n, for n=1:250) as an array to BUGS/JAGS.
